lines.text: This thirty-three second opening swaps my face more than two hundred times.
But watch my eyes. They barely move.
The full cut is at the end. First, here's how I built it.
I'm finishing my master's, and I wanted an opening for a montage of these two years.
On my phone I found eighty-eight videos and two hundred fifty-four photos of myself.
The idea: flash through all of them, with my eyes, nose and mouth locked in one place.
The problem is, every face has a different size and angle.
Stack four of them, and you get a ghost.
Step one, find the face. A landmark model marks four hundred seventy-eight points on it.
I only use six. The eyes, the tip of the nose, the corners of the mouth, and the chin.
Then I fixed one template face, and fitted every photo to it using only scale, rotation and position.
Stack them again, and the ghost is gone.
But a turned head never fits.
So I added gates. Head turned more than eight degrees, out. Eyes closed, out. Mouth wide open, out.
In the end, two hundred cuts came from just forty sources.
Another trap. On paper it was aligned, but the render came out slightly off.
So the code measures the rendered frame, pushes the error back, and repeats.
In 4K, the eyes now land within twelve to eighteen pixels.
Lighting was all over the place. Bright sun, dark rooms.
I measured the skin on every face, evened out brightness and color, then graded everything together.
The music came from a local model. A hundred and twenty beats per minute, with a big drop just after eight seconds.
I extracted every beat. Eighth notes before the drop, sixteenths after, and thirty-second notes at the peak.
I didn't drag clips by hand. Every cut lives in a table. Frame, face, size, color.
A script builds the DaVinci Resolve timeline from that table. Change one rule, and it rebuilds in minutes. This opening went through more than fifteen versions.
Picture in picture shows one feature at a time. One eye, or one mouth.
Split faces join the left half from one day with the right half from another.
For the naked-eye 3D shots, I cut myself out and laid the cutout over two black bars, so I step out of the frame.
The first cutouts had a white halo, and the light didn't match. A finer matting model fixed it.
The ending is the part I cared about most.
One face splits on the beat into two hundred fifty-six bricks. Every brick is an aligned me.
Then the wall breaks, and falls to the floor.
And here, I hold. Nothing moves.
Then the pieces fly back like particles, form a tunnel, and dive into the title.
My first version went straight from wall to tunnel. It felt flat. That one pause is what makes it land.
Plenty went wrong along the way.
The early cuts had white flashes. Rewatching them actually hurt, so I swapped them for warm light.
A thin vertical line ran through the whole video. It came from a film scratch overlay.
And one ending blew out to pure white. You couldn't see a single face.
Looking back, this is the whole pipeline.
AI did a lot of the heavy lifting. Fast, and never tired. But which cut looks right, and where to pause, I had to see for myself, again and again.
Okay. Here's the full cut.
One question. The pause before the tunnel. Keep it, or cut it? Tell me in the comments.
The code, the data and a full tutorial are open source. The link is in the post.
